t: Painted Grey Ware is an archaeologists’ name for a culture identified by its fine grey bowls painted with simple black patterns, found at 1,576 sites in northern India.
Its people farmed with the plough, kept cattle, sheep, pigs and horses, worked iron and ivory, and lived mostly in villages, with several dozen towns.
It probably corresponds to the middle and late Vedic period and the Kuru-Panchala kingdom, and many of its settlements grew into the towns of the Northern Black Polished Ware period.
dyk: The painted grey ware was a luxury: almost all of it is drinking ware, and it makes up only 10–15% of the pottery found from Vedic times, most of the rest being red ware.
ev: Painted Grey Ware appears in the Ghaggar valley and the upper Ganga region (Uesugi’s Period I)
The culture spreads into the western part of the Ganga valley (Uesugi’s Period II)
Northern Black Polished Ware succeeds it, with the rise of the Mahajanapada states
In Uesugi’s Period III the culture interacts with regions to the east
Plain Grey Ware is found at Anuradhapura in Sri Lanka in levels of 600–500 BCE, showing connections with northern India
Excavations at Alamgirpur, near Delhi, reveal an overlap between late Harappan and the earliest Painted Grey Ware levels
Two periods of Painted Grey Ware are identified at Ahichhatra, c. 1500–800 and 800–400 BCE
1,576 Painted Grey Ware sites are known

f.homeland: The western Gangetic plain and the Ghaggar-Hakra valley, with the Sutlej and upper Ganga-Yamuna valleys (Haryana, western Uttar Pradesh, around Delhi); key sites Mathura, Ahichhatra, Jakhera, Bhagwanpura, Alamgirpur, Kampil
f.period: Conventionally c. 1200–600/500 BCE, or 1300–500/300 BCE; Akinori Uesugi’s Period I c. 1300–1000 BCE, Period II c. 1000–600 BCE, Period III c. 600–300 BCE; earlier radiocarbon dates have been reported from single sites
f.known: fine grey drinking ware painted with black geometric patterns; early iron metallurgy in the region; farming villages and some fortified towns; domesticated horses; ivory-working; stamp seals without inscriptions
f.sources: Excavated sites (1,576 known as of 2018) and surveys; radiocarbon dates; the later Vedic literature, which the culture probably corresponds to
